transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. I'm Dr. [Your Name]. What brings you in today?

Hi, Doctor. I’m here because I just… I can’t seem to keep things in order anymore, especially at work. I work in laundry and dry cleaning, and there are always tickets, receipts, notes from the workshop, customer jobs, little slips of paper—everything—and lately it all ends up in piles together. Then I’m standing there looking at it and I don’t even know what I’m supposed to handle first.

It’s not like I’m trying to be careless. I’ll think I’ve put something somewhere sensible, and then later I’m digging through a stack trying to match a receipt to a customer’s job or figure out which note goes with what. It gets embarrassing and stressful, because the work depends on keeping those things straight. That’s really what brought me in.
Can you tell me if you’ve had trouble organizing tasks or activities in other parts of your life, not just at work?

I mean, work is the main place I notice it because it’s right in front of me all day, and there are so many little pieces to keep straight. The tickets, the receipts, the notes from the workshop, the customer jobs—if I don’t keep them in the right place, everything starts blending together.

It’s like I’ll start out thinking, “Okay, this goes here, that goes there,” and then before I know it there’s a pile, and another pile, and I’m looking at it all trying to figure out what I was supposed to do first. That’s the part that really gets me overwhelmed. I don’t even know where to start sometimes.

So… yes, organizing things is the problem, but I guess I’m mostly seeing it with my work tasks because that’s where it causes the biggest trouble.
Do you often find yourself avoiding starting tasks because they feel too overwhelming or do you tend to put things off until the last minute?

I’m not really sure how to answer that, honestly. I don’t think I’ve noticed it as, like, “I’m avoiding this” in a clear way. It’s more that when there are too many things in front of me, especially little separate things that all matter, I can get stuck looking at them and not know what step comes first.

So maybe from the outside it might look like I’m putting it off, but in my head it’s more like I’m trying to sort out where to begin. I’ll stand there thinking, “Okay, I need to deal with this,” but then there’s another thing attached to it, and another thing, and I end up kind of circling around it instead of just starting. I don’t know if that counts as avoiding it or waiting until the last minute. I haven’t really thought of it that way.
Can you think of times outside of work—like at home or with personal tasks—where you’ve had trouble getting started on something even when you knew you needed to?

I’m trying to think of a home example, and honestly my mind keeps going back to the work situation because that’s where it’s so obvious and where it gets me upset. At home, I can have clutter or little things lying around, sure, but it doesn’t stand out to me the same way.

At work it’s more like… there are tickets, receipts, workshop notes, customer jobs, all these bits that are supposed to match up and mean something, and once they start piling together I just freeze a bit. I’ll know I need to start somewhere, but I’m staring at the pile thinking, “Is this receipt for that job? Did this note go with that customer? Which one was supposed to be done first?” And then I don’t know what to handle first.

So outside of work, I’m not sure I can give you a strong example. It’s really the keeping-things-in-order part at work that brought me in.

Can you tell me if you experience similar difficulties with disorganization or getting started on tasks in non-work settings, such as managing personal responsibilities, chores at home, or even following through with plans in your free time?

I know you’re asking about home and personal things, and I’m trying to answer that properly, but I keep coming back to work because that’s the thing that feels like it’s gotten out of control.

It’s not just “messy,” you know? It’s like I’ve got tickets, receipts, notes from the workshop, customer jobs, all these separate pieces that are supposed to match up with each other, and they end up in piles or mixed together. Then I’m standing there trying to figure out what belongs with what, what has to be handled first, what I already did, what still needs to be done… and it just turns into this big tangle in my head.

So with chores at home or free-time plans, I’m not saying I’m perfect, but that’s not really what brought me in. What brought me in is that I can’t seem to keep my work in order anymore, and once it’s all piled together, I don’t know what to handle first. That’s where I really notice the disorganization and getting stuck.
Can you describe if you have similar trouble organizing things, even in small ways, when you're at home or doing personal tasks?

At home, I mean… I’m sure I have little piles or things I don’t put away right away, but it’s harder for me to say it’s the same kind of problem. The thing I keep noticing, and I know I’m repeating myself a bit, is really at work.

That’s where it feels like I just can’t keep things in order anymore. I’ll have tickets, receipts, workshop notes, customer jobs, and they all need to connect to each other somehow, but they end up piled together or mixed up. Then I’m looking at everything and trying to figure out, “Okay, what belongs with what? Which one do I handle first? What am I missing?” And I sort of get stuck there.

So if you’re asking about small things at home, I don’t have a clear example that feels as strong. What brings me in is that at work, once all those papers and job details are together in a pile, I really don’t know what to handle first, and it’s been upsetting because I feel like I should be able to keep it straight.
Can you tell me if you have trouble deciding where to start when you have multiple things to do at home or in your personal life, even if it's something small?

I know you’re asking about home again, and I’m not trying to dodge it, but I honestly keep landing back on the same problem because that’s the one that feels the most real to me.

At home, if there are a few little things to do, I might put something off or leave something sitting there, but I don’t know that I can describe it as clearly. At work, though, it’s like everything depends on me keeping these pieces straight. There are tickets, receipts, notes from the workshop, customer jobs, and they’re all supposed to connect somehow. And once they get piled together, I look at them and I just don’t know where to start.

It’s not even that I don’t understand that something needs to be done. I do. I know I need to sort it out. But then I’m thinking, “Okay, is this receipt for that job? Did this ticket already get handled? Is this customer waiting on something? What goes first?” And the more I look at it, the more tangled it feels. That’s really what brought me in, because I can’t seem to keep my work in order anymore, and then I get stuck trying to decide what to handle first.
When you're faced with a pile of mixed-up work items and you're trying to figure out where to start, do you notice feelings like anxiety, frustration, or sadness coming up for you?

I’m not sure I can name it that clearly. I don’t know if I’d call it anxiety or sadness exactly. In the moment, I’m mostly just… stuck. Like I’m looking at the pile and trying to make my brain sort it into order, and it just won’t line up.

I can tell something is building up in me, but I don’t always stop and think, “This is this feeling” or “that’s that feeling.” It’s more like I get caught in the mess of it — the tickets, receipts, notes, all of it — and I keep thinking I should be able to figure it out, but I can’t get the first step clear.

So, yes, it bothers me, but I’m not sure I have the right word for the feeling. It’s more that I get mentally jammed up, and then I’m just standing there with all of it in front of me.

When you're trying to sort through the pile of work items and you can't figure out where to start, do you notice a strong emotional reaction like anxiety, frustration, or sadness building up inside you?

I don’t know that I’d call it strong, exactly. I mean, maybe from the outside it might look like I’m frustrated, because I’m standing there too long or I’m shuffling the same papers around, but inside I don’t always have a clear feeling word for it.

It’s more like my head gets crowded. I’m looking at the receipts and the tickets and the notes, and I know each one probably belongs to something, but I can’t get them to line up in my mind. Then I start thinking, “If I pick the wrong thing first, I’m going to miss something,” or “What if this customer job is waiting and I don’t realize it?” But I don’t know if that’s anxiety the way you mean it.

I do get bothered by it, yes. I can feel myself getting tense in the sense that I don’t want to be standing there stuck, and I feel kind of embarrassed because it seems like it should be simple. But I’m not sitting there crying or anything like that, and I wouldn’t say sadness is the main thing. It’s mostly this jammed-up, overwhelmed feeling where I can’t get the first step to show itself.
When you're stuck looking at the pile of work items and can't figure out where to start, do you feel a rising sense of pressure or emotional discomfort, even if you can't name the exact feeling?

Yes… I think “pressure” is probably closer than me trying to call it anxiety or sadness. It feels like this pressure starts building because I know those things aren’t just random papers. The tickets, the receipts, the workshop notes, the customer jobs — they all mean something, and they all have to match up right somehow.

And when they’re piled together, I’ll look at it and think, okay, I need to get this in order, but then I can’t tell what should be handled first. Like, do I start with the customer ticket, or the receipt, or the note from the workshop? Did something already get done and I just didn’t connect it? Is somebody waiting because I didn’t sort it out? It turns into this whole knot in my head.

So yes, there’s discomfort. I don’t always have a clean name for it, but I feel it. It’s like I’m standing there knowing I should be able to just organize it and move through it, but I can’t get the first step clear. That’s really the thing that made me come in — I can’t seem to keep my work in order anymore, and once it piles up like that, I don’t know what to handle first.
Can you tell me if you’ve had trouble paying attention or staying focused on tasks in other parts of your life, like at home, in conversations, or while reading or watching something?

Yes, I do, especially with things that don’t keep pulling me back by themselves. At work, I can sit down or stand there and start going over the day’s dry-cleaning orders, and at first I’m fine. I’ll be looking at the slips and trying to check what came in, what needs to go out, what has a special instruction, that kind of thing.

But then, after a few minutes, it’s like my mind has stepped sideways without asking me. I’ll suddenly be thinking about a label on something, or something I’m supposed to do for choir, or something at home I need to remember, and I’m still sort of looking at the orders, but I’m not really taking them in. Then I come back to myself and realize I’ve missed half of what I was supposed to check.

It’s frustrating because I don’t always notice the exact moment I drifted off. I don’t think, “Okay, now I’m not paying attention.” I just realize afterward that I’ve been staring at the papers or going through the motions, and I have to back up and start checking again because I don’t trust that I actually caught everything. So yes, that kind of thing happens outside just the messy pile problem too.
Can you remember if you had similar issues with staying focused or getting organized when you were younger, like in school or when you were a child?

Yes, I can remember that being there when I was little, actually. It wasn’t exactly framed the same way back then, but my mother heard about it from teachers more than once.

They would say things like, “She’s bright, but she’s scattered,” which I remember because that word seemed to follow me around. I could understand the work, but I’d lose the worksheet, or forget to turn something in, or I’d start something and then need to be reminded to finish it. My desk would get messy with papers stuffed in places, and then I’d be digging around for something while everyone else already had theirs out.

And talking, too — I got told about that a lot. Not in a mean way all the time, but I was always blurting things out or talking when I was supposed to wait. Teachers would tell my mother I was a good kid and smart, but that I needed a lot of reminders, and that I had trouble keeping myself organized.

So yes, looking back, it wasn’t just something that started at this job. It was there in grade school, just maybe people thought I was careless or chatty or needed to try harder.

target_item.manifestation: I can start going over the day's dry-cleaning orders just fine, but after a few minutes my mind is off on labels, choir plans, or something at home, and then I realize I missed half of what I was supposed to check.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about trouble paying attention or staying focused across different settings, which most directly matches sustained attention difficulty.

patient.answer:
Yes, I do, especially with things that don’t keep pulling me back by themselves. At work, I can sit down or stand there and start going over the day’s dry-cleaning orders, and at first I’m fine. I’ll be looking at the slips and trying to check what came in, what needs to go out, what has a special instruction, that kind of thing.

But then, after a few minutes, it’s like my mind has stepped sideways without asking me. I’ll suddenly be thinking about a label on something, or something I’m supposed to do for choir, or something at home I need to remember, and I’m still sort of looking at the orders, but I’m not really taking them in. Then I come back to myself and realize I’ve missed half of what I was supposed to check.

It’s frustrating because I don’t always notice the exact moment I drifted off. I don’t think, “Okay, now I’m not paying attention.” I just realize afterward that I’ve been staring at the papers or going through the motions, and I have to back up and start checking again because I don’t trust that I actually caught everything. So yes, that kind of thing happens outside just the messy pile problem too.

inference.note: The patient reported difficulties with attention and focus beyond the workplace, indicating possible ADHD (F90.0). Additionally, the emotional discomfort and pressure experienced when facing disorganized tasks may suggest Adjustment Disorder with Mixed Anxiety and Depressed Mood (F43.20). No clear evidence for Major Depressive Disorder (F32.9) or Other Specified Mental Disorders (F06.7) was established.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient has a history of symptoms before age 12, which is a key criterion for diagnosing ADHD (F90.0).
doctor.question: Can you remember if you had similar issues with staying focused or getting organized when you were younger, like in school or when you were a child?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 1
target_item.manifestation: Even in grade school, my teachers told my mother I was bright but scattered, always talking out of turn, losing papers, and needing reminders to finish my work.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether similar focus or organization problems were present in childhood or school years, which directly assesses onset before age 12.

patient.answer:
Yes, I can remember that being there when I was little, actually. It wasn’t exactly framed the same way back then, but my mother heard about it from teachers more than once.

They would say things like, “She’s bright, but she’s scattered,” which I remember because that word seemed to follow me around. I could understand the work, but I’d lose the worksheet, or forget to turn something in, or I’d start something and then need to be reminded to finish it. My desk would get messy with papers stuffed in places, and then I’d be digging around for something while everyone else already had theirs out.

And talking, too — I got told about that a lot. Not in a mean way all the time, but I was always blurting things out or talking when I was supposed to wait. Teachers would tell my mother I was a good kid and smart, but that I needed a lot of reminders, and that I had trouble keeping myself organized.

So yes, looking back, it wasn’t just something that started at this job. It was there in grade school, just maybe people thought I was careless or chatty or needed to try harder.

inference.note: The patient reported a history of inattention and disorganization dating back to childhood, with symptoms including difficulty staying focused, losing materials, and being described as 'scattered' by teachers. These symptoms persisted into adulthood and are currently causing significant impairment in occupational functioning. The history of childhood symptoms supports the diagnosis of ADHD, predominantly inattentive presentation (F90.0). While the patient also described pressure and emotional discomfort when overwhelmed, there is insufficient evidence to confirm an anxiety disorder (F43.20) as a primary diagnosis at this time.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with chronic difficulties in organization, task initiation, and sustained attention, with onset in childhood and persistence into adulthood, consistent with ADHD, predominantly inattentive presentation. While adjustment symptoms are present in response to work stress, the longitudinal history and pervasive nature of inattention and disorganization are more indicative of F90.0.
